messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: MLR and fit statistics "out of bounds"
parts:
Your scaling correction factor is quite large at 3.40--I have not seen one so large in a long time.  I would guess that you have highly kurtotic data.  You will want to understand the nature of your data--what is driving this extremely large scaling factor.
     You have 37 observed variables and 6 common factors.  Your n is not terribly small for such a model, but it is not at all large.  You want to review the formulas for alternative fit indices like CFI and RMSEA.  As soon as chi-square is smaller than DF, CFI = 1 and RMSEA = exactly.  The TLI above 1.00 might be taken as a sign of overfitting, though you appear to have only 6 common factors and no free residual covariances.
   My advice would be to report the original and robust chi-squares, and the scaling factor, then report the alternative fit indices that go with the robust chi-square.  But you will want to explain how your data earned such a large scaling factor, and also report enough about the parameter estimates so that someone could replicate your analysis.  One way to obtain a good fit is to use weak items with low correlations.  That would be consistent with the rather small baseline model chi-square after scaling correction, again given that your model has 37 observed variables. You will want to show reviewers that this is not the case with your research.
--Ed Rigdon

Thank you very much for your response. Some of my observed variables are kurtotic and I will look into how this is driving the scaling factor in more detail, as suggested. Although I do have 37 observed variables, I have more than six factors. I included the model syntax below. I just wanted to check that I am not mis-specifying something since the number of observed variables and factors you derived from the output was different than what I have in my model syntax.
Thanks again!
Diana

outcomescfa2<-'
assert=~w1ed_oa_as1 +   w1ed_oa_as3 + w1ed_oa_as4 +   w1ed_oa_as6 + w1ed_ra_as1 +   w1ed_ra_as3 + w1ed_ra_as4 +   w1ed_ra_as6
aggressO=~w1ed_oa_oag1 +  w1ed_oa_oag3 + w1ed_ra_oag1 + w1ed_ra_oag3 
AggressR=~   w1ed_oa_rag2 +   w1ed_oa_rag4 +   w1ed_ra_rag2 +  w1ed_ra_rag4
neuAdult=~w1ed_oa_neu1 + w1ed_oa_neu3 + w1ed_ra_neu1 + w1ed_ra_neu3
neuComf=~ w1ed_oa_neu2 + w1ed_oa_neu4 + w1ed_ra_neu2 + w1ed_ra_neu4

OV =~ w1ov1 + w1ov2 + w1ov3 
RV =~ w1rv1 + w1rv2 + w1rv3
OA=~oa_ave
RA=~ra_ave
accept =~ w1like
reject =~ w1dislike
pop=~ w1pop
unpop=~ w1notpop
depress =~ cesdmean
'
#robust
fitoutcomescfa2robust<- cfa(outcomescfa2, data=data, missing='fiml', std.lv=T, meanstructure=T,  estimator="MLR",control=list(iter.max=100000000))

messages.subject: Re: MLR and fit statistics "out of bounds"
parts:
My mistake--some glitch while I was calculating.  7 multiple indicator factors covering 30 observed variables is more in the typical range.  The 7 single indicator factors could more small values in the correlation matrix of the observed variables than one would have expected if every factor had multiple indicators.  The baseline chi-square value is, again, a bit smaller than I might have expected for a model with 37 observed variables.  If you have many observed variables with just a few response categories--or have responses falling in just a few categories, as when responses are heavily skewed--this might also contribute to both the high hurtosis and the low correlations between observed variables.
--Ed Rigdon
